planting.note: Plant a small container-grown grafted tree in spring or fall into moist, well-drained soil, siting it where it gets some afternoon shade so the variegated leaves resist summer scorch.

directions: Discovered as a chance seedling by Theodore Klein and honored with a Klein Plant Award, Silver Cloud is a striking variegated sport of the eastern redbud, its heart-shaped leaves irregularly blotched with white over soft green, emerging chartreuse in spring and turning soft yellow in fall. Give it consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun to light shade, since the reduced chlorophyll in the variegated tissue makes leaves more prone to bleaching and scorch in hot, exposed sites than the plain green species; deeper variegation actually develops in partial shade. Typical rosy-pink pea flowers still appear on bare branches in early spring, followed by the emerging variegated foliage. As a grafted selection it should be purchased as a named cultivar rather than grown from seed, which will not come true.
sources: University of Kentucky Nursery Crop Extension

planting.note: Set out a container-grown tree in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; this sterile hybrid sets no seed pods, so no litter cleanup is needed after bloom.

directions: Pink Pom Poms is a double-flowered redbud bred by Dr. Dennis Werner at North Carolina State University's JC Raulston Arboretum, a cross of the double-flowered Cercis canadensis 'Flame' and Cercis texensis 'Oklahoma' that produces dense, ruffled clusters of rose-pink blossoms covering bare branches before the foliage emerges. Because the flowers are sterile, the tree never forms the bean-like seed pods typical of redbuds, giving it a tidier look through summer and fall, and its large, glossy green leaves turn brilliant yellow in autumn. It performs best in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though part shade helps in hot summer climates, and it needs a proper winter chill for flowers to set well. Its smaller stature compared to seed-grown redbuds makes it a good fit for foundation plantings and smaller garden spaces.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped tree in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; keep it evenly watered through its first two seasons while the narrow root system establishes.

directions: Selected by Edward Losely from a group of Amelanchier canadensis seedlings and sold as Rainbow Pillar, this strongly columnar serviceberry stays only 8-10 feet wide while reaching 15-20 feet tall, making it useful as a narrow street tree, screen, or vertical accent where a spreading serviceberry would not fit. It carries the same white spring flower clusters, edible red-to-purple June berries beloved by birds (and usable in pastries and preserves), and vivid multi-colored fall foliage as its wide-crowned relatives, with foliage that is notably unaffected by powdery mildew. Grow it in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and expect it to tolerate the occasional dry spell once established. Because it is a patented, propagated clone, buy named plants rather than seedlings to guarantee the columnar habit.

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall directly where the tree is to grow, since the deep taproot resents later transplanting; protect young seedlings from browsing deer and rabbits.

directions: Engelmann Oak, also called Mesa Oak, is a slow-growing, semi-deciduous oak restricted to a narrow range of foothill woodlands in southern California and northern Baja California, where habitat loss has made it a species of conservation concern. Its blue-green, leathery, sparsely toothed leaves and broad, rounded crown make it a distinctive presence in coastal sage and chaparral-edge plantings. Once established it is very drought tolerant and should be grown on lean, well-drained soil with minimal summer irrigation to avoid root disease. Its acorns are an important food source for deer, woodpeckers, and other wildlife across its limited native range.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall in rocky, well-drained soil typical of oak woodland; this species tolerates thin, alkaline soils poorly suited to eastern oaks.

directions: Arizona White Oak is a dominant evergreen tree of the Madrean oak woodlands (the 'encinal' zone) of southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, forming broad, rounded canopies of gray-green, leathery leaves over rocky foothill slopes. It is highly drought tolerant once established and thrives in the alkaline, well-drained soils typical of its native mountain range country, needing little to no irrigation beyond the first few years. Its acorns are an important seasonal food source for deer, javelina, and numerous bird species, and the tree provides critical shade and cover in otherwise open desert grassland-woodland transition zones. It grows slowly, so choose a permanent site with full sun and good drainage from the start.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall in gravelly, sharply drained soil; growth is slow, so protect seedlings from grazing and drought stress for the first several years.

directions: Gray Oak takes its name from the dusty, gray-green cast of its small, leathery, evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves, and it forms an important part of pinyon-juniper and oak woodland communities across west Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona into northern Mexico. It ranges from a large multi-stemmed shrub to a rounded medium tree depending on site conditions, favoring rocky limestone slopes and canyon sides with excellent drainage. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it needs no supplemental irrigation in its native range and should be planted in full sun on lean soil. Its acorns provide reliable forage for deer, javelina, and many bird species in an otherwise sparse high-desert landscape.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns 1 inch deep in fall in well-drained, rocky canyon or foothill soil; young trees establish a deep taproot and should not be transplanted once rooted.

directions: Emory Oak, known locally as bellota, is a dark-leaved evergreen oak of southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, and northern Mexico's mid-elevation canyons and foothills, valued both ecologically and culturally. Unlike most oaks, its acorns are sweet rather than bitter and have long been harvested as a food staple by Apache and O'odham communities, in addition to being a major forage source for deer, javelina, and turkey. It tolerates rocky, thin, well-drained soils and needs little water once its deep taproot is established, making it well suited to xeric foothill plantings. Give it full sun and room to develop its dense, rounded, glossy-leaved canopy over what is typically a slow-growing but long-lived tree.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
